title: Remove Colored Pieces if Both Neighbors are the Same Color
statement:
A row of pieces is described by the string `colors`, where `colors[i]` is `'A'` or `'B'`, the color of the piece at position `i`. Alice and Bob play a game on this row, taking turns with Alice going first. On each turn the current player deletes one piece from the row, after which the remaining pieces close the gap:

- Alice may delete only an `'A'` piece whose left and right neighbors are both `'A'`.
- Bob may delete only a `'B'` piece whose left and right neighbors are both `'B'`.
- The first and last pieces of the row can never be deleted, since they lack a neighbor on one side.
- A player who has no legal deletion on their turn loses, and the other player wins.

If both play optimally, return `true` when Alice wins and `false` when Bob wins.
constraints: colors contains only the letters 'A' and 'B'
notes:
## Intuition

Searching the game tree (every possible deletion on every turn) is correct but explodes quickly. The key observation is that the two players never interfere with each other. Alice can only delete an `'A'` from the inside of a run of at least three `'A'`s, and doing so leaves that run at least two long, so the neighboring `'B'` runs never merge or change. The same holds for Bob. A run of length `len` therefore gives its owner exactly `len - 2` moves no matter what anyone does, which is the number of positions inside it whose two neighbors match. Alice runs out first when her total is not larger than Bob's, so she wins exactly when she has strictly more moves.

## Approach

1. Set `aliceMoves` and `bobMoves` to 0.
2. For every inner index `i` (not the first or last), read the neighbors `left` and `right`.
3. Skip `i` unless both neighbors equal `colors[i]`.
4. Otherwise it is one available move: add it to `aliceMoves` for `'A'`, to `bobMoves` for `'B'`.
5. Return `aliceMoves > bobMoves`.

## Example 1, step by step

For `colors = "AAABABB"`, only `i = 1` has matching neighbors (`A A A`), so `aliceMoves = 1`. At `i = 5` the piece is `'B'` but its left neighbor is `'A'`, so `bobMoves` stays 0. Since `1 > 0`, the answer is `true`: Alice moves once and Bob is stuck.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the string.
- Space: O(1): two counters.

## Pitfalls

- A tie means Bob wins: when both have the same number of moves, Alice is the first to run out, so use a strict `>`.
- Edge pieces are never removable, so the loop runs from 1 to `colors.length - 2`.
- Do not simulate deletions; the counts are fixed from the start because the players cannot affect each other.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `aliceMoves` | number of `'A'` pieces Alice will be able to remove |
| `bobMoves` | number of `'B'` pieces Bob will be able to remove |
| `i` | index of the piece being checked |
| `left`, `right` | colors of the neighbors of piece `i` |

narration.2: Count how many deletions Alice will be able to make in total.
narration.3: Count Bob's total deletions the same way.
narration.5: Check every piece except the two ends, which can never be removed.
narration.6: Read the color of the piece on the left...
narration.7: ...and the color of the piece on the right.
narration.8: If either neighbor differs from this piece, nobody can ever delete it.
narration.11: All three pieces match; check whether they are A pieces.
narration.12: They are, so this is one more deletion Alice can make.
narration.14: Otherwise the three pieces are all B, which is one more deletion for Bob.
narration.17: Moves are independent, so Alice wins exactly when she has strictly more of them than Bob.
